newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: COLOMBIAN FINANCIERS SEES FOREIGN INVESTMENT SLIDE.
newsitem.headline: COLOMBIAN FINANCIERS SEES FOREIGN INVESTMENT SLIDE.

text.p: Foreign investment flows into Colombia could drop by more than half by the year 2000 if the government fails to establish more favorable conditions, a leading financial group said Monday.
The National Association of Financial Institutions (ANIF) called for beefed up legislation to protect foreign investment and for improved contract terms for oil companies.
In its weekly report, ANIF predicted foreign investment inflows could drop from an estimated $3.9 billion this year to less than $1.7 billion per year after 2000.
"Our ability to continue attracting foreign investment is fundamental to this country...A good climate for foreign investment can only be assured if we offer competitive conditions," ANIF said.

Under the Colombian constitution, foreign investments can theoretically be expropriated without compensation, which U.S. diplomats have regularly said is deterring higher levels of U.S. investment in the country.
ANIF also criticized what it said were unfavorable contract terms for foreign oil companies operating in Colombia in association with the state-run oil company Ecopetrol.

British multinational, British Petroleum Co Plc, Colombia's largest single foreign investor, is currently involved in a protracted wrangle over the terms of production at the giant Piedemonte field in the eastern plains region.

BP has said the current deal coupled with notoriously difficult drilling conditions has cut potential margins to the bone and has called for the contract to be redefined to allow it a bigger share of the profits.
An increasing number of attacks by leftist rebels on the country's key oil infrastructure may also frighten away new foreign investment, ANIF said.
